column2: When the boats reached Hangzhou, Wang rested briefly at home, changed into official robes, and went to see the governor. He personally reported the journey and presented a letter from Huang's family acknowledging safe receipt of the twenty thousand taels. Both the public and private aspects of the assignment had been handled handsomely. Huang was exceedingly pleased. “You've worked hard. I know what you've done,” he said. “I have plans of my own. You'll hear something within a few days.” “Yes, Your Excellency.” Wang dared not inquire further. Leaving the governor's yamen, he went to call on Treasurer Lingui. Knowing how difficult Huang could be, Lingui had previously treated Wang rather like a spirit best respected from a distance. Whether things went well or badly, someone taller would hold up the falling sky. He sought no merit, only freedom from blame and trouble. Now Wang's tactful, thorough handling of the journey, together with his understanding of the “rules,” had exceeded Lingui's hopes. Zhou's praise made him regard Wang more highly still. As soon as the visiting card went in, a message came out: “Ask His Honour Wang to change into ordinary clothes and meet me in my private office.” This was how one received an intimate friend of roughly equal standing. Wang knew that Zhou's favourable account had produced the result, and that Hu deserved the credit for winning Zhou over. Thinking of Hu and of Lingui's exceptional courtesy, he suddenly had an idea: he would ask Lingui to recommend Hu for advancement.

They met in ordinary clothes in the private office. The Manchus were ceremonious, and Lingui took Wang's hand, asked whether the journey had gone smoothly and whether everyone at home was well, then, after these affectionate greetings, led him into the western room. The office occupied a small courtyard, with a single-storey building of three rooms: an open central reception room and an enclosed room on either side. Documents were signed and business conducted in the eastern room; the western was Lingui's everyday sitting room. As the curtain lifted, Wang saw an opium tray on a rosewood couch. A maid with a long plait and slender waist had just lit a bright Taigu lamp. “Please,” Lingui said, indicating the upper end of the couch. “You take it, Your Excellency.” Wang smiled. “I don't know how to enjoy that pleasure.” “It's just as well that you don't.” Lingui dispensed with polite pretence. “In truth, the stuff does more harm than good. But you can lie down and keep me company.” That was harmless enough. Provided one did not become addicted, conversation beside an opium tray could be entertaining, and lying head to head across the little flame could deepen a friendship. Wang readily agreed and reclined at the lower end. The pretty maid immediately held his feet, removed his boots, arranged a square stool beneath them, and covered his lower body with a Russian blanket.

Another maid brought four small dishes of fruit and two exquisite little teapots. Setting them beside the tray, she sat on a low stool to prepare the opium. Once a pipe was filled, she offered its jade-inlaid ivory stem to Wang's lips. “Give it to your master. I don't smoke.” Lingui accepted without ceremony, finished the pipe in one sustained breath, drank from the hot teapot, and put a pine-nut sweet into his mouth. Then, slowly letting smoke escape through his nostrils, he closed his eyes as though transported. “Brother Xuexuan,” he began, turning to business, “you've done Zhejiang great credit on this journey. If all official business went as smoothly as yours, I could live comfortably.” “It was entirely due to Your Excellency's support. Subordinates can act freely only when their superiors trust them.” “One must first feel secure before allowing a free hand. Frankly, I couldn't feel more secure about you. With the governor standing behind everything, whatever you propose is acceptable.” Lingui added, “The governor is a shrewd man too. If he puts himself in my position, he's certain to look after me.” He smoked a second pipe. Wang considered his words and concluded that the latter remark meant he must not forget Lingui's proper share while attending to the governor. In fact, there was no need to say it: Hu had already thought of that.

But Wang had learned one principle of official life: anything not meant for outsiders' knowledge must be kept completely secret. Though they faced each other on the same couch, the presence of the maid preparing the pipe prevented him from making any sign. “Quite so,” he answered. “There are two sorts of superior one hopes to serve. The best is naturally someone like Your Excellency, generous, tolerant, and considerate of his subordinates. Failing that, I would prefer Governor Huang. Shrewd though he is, he certainly knows merit from fault and right from wrong.” “Merit from fault, perhaps. Right from wrong—not necessarily.” Lingui regretted the remark as soon as he made it. “Brother Xuexuan,” he added with deliberate irony, “you might mention these words to the governor when you have a chance.” Wang was quick to respond. “That is an honour I must decline!” he said with a smile. “I never care to carry tales behind people's backs. It causes needless trouble, harms others, and benefits oneself not at all. Why do it?” The answer impressed Lingui deeply. This man truly knew how to handle every situation. He could be trusted.

With his last psychological guard removed, Lingui spoke without reserve and with increasing pleasure. He discussed conditions in the capital and the rules and precedents of the six ministries, greatly enlarging Wang's knowledge. Finally he returned to official business. “We must press ahead with this year's new grain. Jiangsu and Zhejiang bear exceptionally heavy tax quotas, yet Zhejiang is really no match for Jiangsu. How can Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou compare with Suzhou, Songjiang, and Taicang? Of our three prefectures, Huzhou is the richest, but its affairs are the hardest to manage.” He sighed. “The prefect of Huzhou has been dismissed for delaying the grain, and for the moment I can't find anyone to take over. A real headache!” Chunshou had lost his life over Huzhou, so Lingui could not help being wary. Wang understood the difficulty, but feared that pursuing it would lead to Chunshou's case and all its awkward implications. He merely listened. “I do have an idea!” Lingui suddenly exclaimed, then fell silent. After a long pause, he answered himself. “No. It won't work. There's no precedent.” Wang could not imagine what he meant, but it was not his place to ask. During the ensuing silence, Lingui finished his twenty-fourth pipe and ordered dinner. The maids went out to pass on the instruction. With nobody else present, Wang could produce what he had brought.

“I've brought Your Excellency a little curiosity.” From an inner pocket he took a paper parcel and passed it across the opium lamp. Inside was an exquisite wallet of exceptionally soft leather. Its pattern immediately showed that it came from the West. Lingui examined the outside and was about to open it when Wang spoke again. “Perhaps later.” Plainly there was something special within. Lingui smiled, thanked him, and put it away. When dinner was served, he excused himself, slipped outside, and opened it privately. The wallet held a bank draft for five thousand taels. Wang had acted in great secrecy, but Lingui showed no concern about his servants. Returning to invite his guest to the table, his first words were, “I am much indebted to you. What about the grain intendant?” “A little something for him too.” “How much?” “Three.” He meant three thousand taels. Lingui nodded. “Delivered already?” “Not yet. Naturally, I had to call on Your Excellency before visiting him.” “It's too late today. Go early tomorrow. He takes these matters very seriously.”

The tone was that of affectionate advice to one of his own people. Wang felt that their relationship had advanced another step. “Thank you for the guidance, Your Excellency,” he answered gratefully. “Could you put away that ‘Your Excellency’?” Lingui set down his wine cup and frowned. “It's unbearably commonplace and spoils the pleasure of drinking.” Wang smiled. “Obedience is better than ceremony. I shall call you Mr Lin, with every respect. Let us drink a cup!” “Excellent!” Lingui drank gladly, then continued, “I hadn't finished what I was saying. Do you know the grain intendant's particular passion?” “No. I must ask you to enlighten me.” “In fact, everyone shares it, but his case is exceptional.” Lingui smiled. “He loves what lies beneath a man's knees.” Wang was baffled by the riddle. “Your learning is as broad as the sea. Can this unfinished proverb defeat you?” So that was it! The saying ran, “There is gold beneath a man's knees.” The unspoken words were “there is gold.” The Manchus' attempts at literary wit could sometimes be oddly contrived. Wang was genuinely amused.

“So I advise you not to send a bank draft. Exchange it for gold leaf.” Lingui could scarcely suppress his amusement. “They say he delights in counting his gold sheets every night before bed. Otherwise he feels something is missing and cannot sleep peacefully.” “That is a curious habit. What happens when he travels?” Wang asked. “Does he take the gold with him? Wouldn't that invite thieves?” “That I don't know.” Their joking over, they returned to business. Lingui asked about official circles in Shanghai. Wang told him of Ni's grievances and complaints and his own promise to look after Ni's family. “I can say nothing about that,” Lingui replied. “I can't even concern myself with Ni's family. I know how suspicious the governor is.”

“Yes.” “So I advise you to look after them discreetly and keep it from the governor.” Lingui lowered his voice. “I truly don't understand why our Mr Huang is so harsh. What has the treasurer of Jiangsu to do with the governor of Zhejiang? Why torment him like that? And there's something else, even less defensible...” At the crucial point he stopped. Plainly the matter was important enough that Wang's status as Huang's favourite still troubled him. Understanding this, Wang thought it better not to press. He raised his cup and considered how to change the subject. Lingui, however, felt embarrassed. “I may as well tell you. He's done something to benefit himself at another man's expense. Looking after oneself is natural enough, but one ought to consider whom one harms. To injure a man from one's own examination cohort is hardly generous.” Which fellow graduate had Huang injured? Their cohort's remarkable advancement depended upon mutual support. Had Huang himself not relied upon Grand Councillor Peng Yunzhang and He Guiqing to intercede and shield him in the case of Chunshou's forced suicide? Wang therefore half doubted Lingui's story.

“There was an edict recently about the defence of Jiangsu and Zhejiang,” Lingui asked. “Did you see it?” “No. I was in Shanghai and haven't read the court bulletins for some time.” “It said: ‘Governor Huang Zonghan of Zhejiang reports the dispatch of troops to Jiangsu and arrangements for preventing an incursion into Zhejiang.’ The imperial response was: ‘Excellent. In the present military affairs, submit any useful observations you may have without distinguishing between the concerns of one province and another.’” Wang listened with surprise and delight. Sending troops beyond the provincial boundary to meet the enemy had been his suggestion. Huang had adopted it—and, more unexpectedly, received imperial praise! He therefore felt bound to defend it. “There seems nothing wrong with sending troops beyond the province.” “Indeed! Nobody says there is. But an official of Zhejiang should attend to Zhejiang's affairs. Even if the edict says not to distinguish between provinces, we must observe proper limits and not take over another man's duties. Yet Governor Huang sends memorial after memorial, indiscriminately telling the throne how Jiangsu's military affairs should be arranged. Tell me,” Lingui leaned forward, “if you were governor of Jiangsu, how would you feel?” Now Wang understood. For the sake of imperial favour, Huang was leaving no room for his fellow graduate Xu Naizhao, governor of Jiangsu. That was indefensible. His conduct also suggested an ambition to be transferred there. If so, it was still less wise. Jiangsu was certainly one of the empire's richest regions, but war made it an undesirable posting. If an opportunity arose, Wang ought to advise him against it.

Unaware of these further thoughts, Lingui mistook Wang's silence for disagreement. He asked frankly, “Brother Xuexuan, what do you think of what I've said?” Wang came to himself and hurried to prevent a misunderstanding. “Your Excellency's intentions are generous, and your view is naturally just. Unfortunately, my position is too insignificant for my words to carry weight. Otherwise I would find an opportunity to advise him.” “No need!” Lingui waved his hands. “I'm speaking in confidence because I regard you as a good friend. Nobody else need hear of it.” “Of course.” Wang was solemn. “I wouldn't dare repeat a word of what you've said. But since the matter appears in a publicly issued edict, even if I spoke to the governor, he would have no reason to suspect anyone else.” “That is up to you. The Xu family is prominent in Hangzhou, but has no connection with me. I'm merely judging the matter and speaking fairly.” The subject was dropped. They had drunk enough, so Wang asked his host for rice, ate, and took his leave. Knowing that he had only just returned and must have much to do at home, Lingui did not detain him. He personally escorted him to the middle gate, and they parted in good spirits.

Wang spent the following day making more calls, bringing gifts to everyone with whom he had even a slight acquaintance. Coming from Shanghai, these “local products” were in fact foreign goods. Maritime trade had only recently opened. Objects worth little in their Western countries became rare treasures in China. Even a linen handkerchief won unusual appreciation. The round of visits therefore gained Wang many more friends. When he returned home that evening, Hu was in the reception room, joking with his young son. They had been apart for only a day, yet Wang felt as though meeting an old friend after years of separation, with a great deal he urgently wished to say. “Have you eaten?” “No. I meant to invite you up City God Hill for yousuobing cakes, but it's too late now.” The suggestion appealed to Wang. “Not too late! The summer solstice is approaching, the days are long, and the weather is warm. Even if it gets late, it doesn't matter. How shall we go?” “Surely not with gongs and cries to clear the road!” Hu laughed. Wang was amused too. “Naturally, I'll change into ordinary clothes. I meant that we needn't even take a chair or servants. We can walk.” “Good. Put on dark crystal spectacles, and you needn't greet acquaintances if we meet any.” Wang changed into a sapphire-blue satin robe with a dark tribute-satin waistcoat, light cotton socks, and double-ridged shoes. Wearing his large dark spectacles and carrying a folding fan, he walked with Hu through Dajing Lane and straight up City God Hill, both looking at ease.

“Let's have tea where we first met,” Wang said. “A gentleman doesn't forget his beginnings. We ought to give him some good custom today.” By “him,” he meant the proprietor of the tea place. This was Wang's second visit with Hu, but his circumstances and state of mind were worlds apart from the first. Once seated, he looked about calmly and contentedly. Less than a year had passed; the lake and hills were unchanged, yet to his eyes they seemed transformed. West Lake, the beautiful Xizi, looked more graceful, and the green hills more charming. “Wine or tea, gentlemen?” Their bearing and clothes made the proprietor unwilling to neglect them, and he came himself. “Both.” Wang imitated the Hangzhou accent. “The new tea is on sale. Tell us what good leaves you have.” “I don't dare keep anything too costly in stock. I'd have to buy it specially.” “No need for that.” After thinking for a long time, Wang said, “Bring a pot of chrysanthemum tea.” The proprietor found him odd. He had begun by asking for fine tea and ended with chrysanthemums. Apparently he was a man of grand words and small expenditure.

Hu too was surprised. “Why chrysanthemum?” “It took me a while to remember. That's what I drank last year.” Only Hu understood. The recollection stirred him as well, but his nature was to look ahead, with little time for the past. He quickly set it aside and ordered the meal. “One chicken prepared three ways; vinegar fish prepared daibin. Do you have a live crucian carp, about a jin in weight?” “I can get one from below the hill. For soup?” “Yes, crucian carp in milky broth. Warm two bowls of Zhuyeqing, bring four small dishes and a few yousuobing cakes, and we'll begin.” “Certainly. They'll be here at once.” When the tea arrived, Wang held his cup and gazed at the dark blue-green and pale purple of the evening haze. Remembering his circumstances here the previous year, he was suddenly overcome by feeling. “Xueyan,” he said with great force, “with the two of us together, what couldn't we accomplish? We must really make something of it.” “That's my thought too. It's what I came to discuss with you today.”

“Tell me!” “I still want to return to my old trade.” “Not to Xinhe, I hope?” Wang was half joking. In truth, he did fear that Xinhe's proprietor might persuade Hu to return. “I've already said it: I won't be bean curd warmed over in the same broth, and I mean to set up for myself. With the war, silver prices are constantly moving. With sound judgement, one can profit on both buying and selling. We mustn't miss the opportunity.” Wang said nothing. His chopsticks moved incessantly over a dish of sprouted beans. Hu knew it was not fondness for the dish: he was calculating. Naturally, he was thinking about capital. There was no need, for Hu had already planned where it would come from. But he could not conveniently say so first. Wang eventually spoke. “Xueyan, frankly, I don't want you opening a bank just now. I need your help, and helping me means helping yourself. Couldn't you purchase an official qualification and stay with me wherever I go? The governor has already spoken of another arrangement shortly. Presumably he'll give me an additional assignment, and then I'll need help all the more. You can't stand aside and watch me neglect one thing while attending to another.” “I've thought of that already. Opening a bank is one matter, helping you another. I can manage both. Rest assured.” “Of course. Nobody knows your ability better than I. Naturally I trust you...”

Seeing that his words did not match his continuing reluctance, Hu lowered his voice. “You've only just begun to succeed, Mr Xuexuan. Frankly, people outside don't yet know much about you. That's precisely why this is the moment for me to open a bank. Once every official and merchant in Zhejiang knows His Honour Wang, and everyone knows our relationship, what will they say if I open one then?” “Only that I supplied the capital. There's no need to conceal our friendship. My financing a bank for you would be perfectly ordinary.” “True. But as the saying goes, only a mediocre man never arouses envy. If we could avoid it and deliberately invite it instead, we'd be foolish. People would say you were using public money for private profit. Someone might amuse himself by filing an accusation against you. How could I feel at ease then?” This struck home. Wang felt the danger could not be ignored and hesitated. “Things must be done without leaving obvious traces.” Hu spoke still more quietly. “A bank has one particular advantage: it can act for circuit and county treasuries. Public funds bear no interest, so they're effectively capital borrowed for nothing. Sooner or later you'll receive a local appointment. If I open a bank then and immediately take over your treasury's business, the connection will be too obvious. That's why I must act now. Do you understand?” “Ah!” Wang saw the matter differently. “I understand.”

“Perhaps not all the subtleties yet. Different trades are separated as though by mountains. Let me explain.” Hu's plan was to establish a firm first, however modest its resources. Outwardly it must look busy and prosperous; inwardly it would have little substance. Once Wang was appointed to a department or county, the bank would handle its treasury business. Public funds being remitted to the provincial capital would flow in continuously, turning appearance into reality. “Brilliant!” Wang laughed and imitated the Hangzhou accent. “Xueyan, you really know how to perform conjuring tricks!” “A trick is still an illusion. One or two may be useful; too many lose their value. What matters is eventually producing something real.” “That's sound sense.” Wang stopped laughing and spoke seriously. “Let us plan it. First, how much capital is needed?”

Over wine, they discussed opening the bank. The main question was the source of capital, which first required a reckoning of the official-procurement affair. Hu had an extraordinary memory and calculated rapidly in his head. Item by item, the account came to a deficit of more than fourteen thousand taels, all entered in Xinhe's books. To obtain so desirable an assignment at the Sea Transport Bureau, gain nothing from it, and instead incur a deficit seemed hard to justify. Wang, however, did not mind. It was an investment. Judged by the achievements of the past two months and the connections established on every side, the return was already considerable. Yet finding capital for a bank on top of this debt seemed difficult. “If we announce capital of two hundred thousand taels, even a quarter actually paid in means fifty thousand. That may be a strain just now.” “We don't need fifty thousand,” Hu said. “Twenty thousand at most. For the moment, we need a few thousand to establish a proper appearance.” “A few thousand is available at any time. I'll transfer it to you at once.” “Then we're set. There's also a price-difference allowance of several tens of thousands to draw from the provincial treasury. It was meant for Tongyu, but we can hold it back for a while.” “Yes!” Wang saw the point. “Tongyu has borrowed a hundred thousand, and we've secretly guaranteed it. A little delay in paying this allowance isn't unreasonable.” “Exactly. But drawing it from the treasury will take several months unless we work through the right connections.”

Wang understood that well. Even the most urgently needed military pay faced obstruction at every stage before release. The treasury clerks were particularly difficult. “‘The King of Hell is easy to see; his little demons are hard to manage!’” he said. “I can deal with Treasurer Lin, but I don't yet see a way through the clerks below him.” “Leave them to me.” Hu was about to say, “You go and see the King of Hell; I'll deal with the demons.” Then he remembered that telling someone to see the King of Hell was an ill-omened joke. He answered plainly instead. “Send an official document pressing for payment. I'll find a way among the subordinates. At worst, it will mean a little more in gratuities.” With that settled, Wang drew five thousand taels from the bureau's public funds the following day and handed it to Hu. The money was available, but smooth progress required people too. If Hu were merely opening a bank and could attend to it himself all day, the lack of a good assistant would not matter for the moment. But he had to coordinate matters in many directions and could not be tied down by daily business. He therefore needed a capable, trustworthy manager.

Two former colleagues at Xinhe had promise, but he did not want to approach them. First, he would be taking good men from Zhang. Neither the obligations of the trade nor their personal friendship permitted it. Second, they knew his background too well. They had joked together as equals. Suddenly becoming employer and employees would embarrass him and make it difficult for them to regard him with proper respect. After much thought, he remembered another man in the trade with whom he had little personal connection. He worked at the counter of a bank in Qinghefang. Hu had dealt with him once and found him clear-headed, with an appearance and manner of speaking well above the ordinary. He was worth recruiting. Zhang would be the best person to approach him. That brought up another problem. Ever since deciding to open a bank on the return voyage from Shanghai, Hu had wondered whether to tell Zhang first or wait until everything was ready and an auspicious opening date selected. A moment's serious thought made the answer plain. Early disclosure might bring no benefit, but late disclosure would certainly do harm. It would first suggest a lack of friendship, as though he were concealing something, and invite suspicion. Zhang was currently bearing substantial risks for him and Wang. Any loss of trust would cause trouble. Besides, gathering staff and opening a bank could not be kept secret. If Zhang discovered it and came to ask, the position would be more awkward still.

Having decided, Hu made a special visit to Xinhe at Salt Bridge. Their meeting was cordial. After chatting in the shop, he said, “Mr Zhang, I have something important to discuss,” and glanced around. “Come inside.” Zhang led him to his bedroom. It was small, and a safe recently purchased from a foreign firm in Shanghai made it more cramped still. They sat on the bed. “Mr Zhang, I've decided to establish a firm of my own.” “Excellent!” Zhang's pleasure sounded somewhat forced. Hu understood: he feared that Hu's bank would affect Xinhe's business. Its dealings with the Sea Transport Bureau were naturally likely to change. He therefore began with reassurance. “Don't worry. A rabbit doesn't eat the grass beside its own burrow. If I meant to take your business, I wouldn't be telling you first. The bureau's dealings will remain with Xinhe. I'll find a different path.” “Oh? What path?” “That will emerge in time. In short, whatever business Xinhe is pursuing, I'll keep clear of it.” “Good.” Their relationship had changed, and Zhang no longer offered insincere courtesies. He answered frankly. “I trust your character. If you're willing to make that concession, I appreciate it. Whatever help I can give, I'll give wholeheartedly. Tell me what you need.”

“Naturally, I must ask your help. First, support me on opening day.” “That goes without saying. I'll bring fellow bankers to make a show of deposits. I can't promise a great deal, but there'll be ten thousand taels or so in silver.” “Excellent. Thank you in advance. Second, I've made it a rule not to take any of Xinhe's good men. I've found someone else and would like you to help bring us together.” “Who?” “At Dayuan in Qinghefang there's a young fellow, surnamed Liu, I think. A presentable man who knows how to deal with people. I'd like to meet him.” “Liu? Presentable?” Zhang frowned in thought, then remembered. “You have a good eye. But I know both Dayuan's proprietor and its manager well, so I can't intervene openly. I'll have someone arrange a meeting. If it works out, you mustn't reveal that I brought you together.”

“I understand.” Zhang had not spoken idly. He did all he could to help and immediately asked someone to contact Liu. That night, close to the second watch, a visitor knocked at Hu's house. Hu took an oil lamp to the door and raised it towards the man's face. It was Liu. “Mr Hu, Mr Zhang of Xinhe asked me to call.” “Yes, indeed. Come inside.” Once they were in the reception room, Hu asked his full name. It was Liu Qingsheng, and Hu addressed him as “Brother Qingsheng.” “Where is your family home?” “Yuyao.” “Ah, a fine place! I've been there,” Hu said with interest. They discussed Yuyao's sights and customs, moved on to Ningbo, then back to Shaoxing. Hu spoke endlessly on every imaginable subject, bewildering Liu. Several times Liu tried to return to the purpose of the visit and asked how he could be of service. Hu always gave a brief, evasive answer and wandered off again, as though bored by the long night and wanting someone to listen to fantastic tales from the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

Liu grew increasingly puzzled and somewhat annoyed. But he too had great perseverance. Neither Hu nor Wang ever told others the story of their remarkable connection. Zhang, however, knew half or more of it and embellished it freely in conversation. Everyone in the trade therefore knew Hu as an unfathomable man of consequence. Liu thought, “He must have a reason for bringing me here. I mean to see what he has to say.” That decision enabled him to endure. Hu was testing precisely that patience. After an hour of empty talk, Liu showed no irritation. Satisfied, Hu considered the first test—and in truth the hardest—passed. Only then did he turn to banking. An expert himself, he disguised his examination as casual conversation and set difficult questions. Liu answered to the best of his knowledge, mostly correctly. The second test was passed as well.

“Brother Qingsheng, I've been away from banking for some time. How many firms are there in the city now?” “Eight large banks. There are more of the smaller establishments: thirty-three altogether.” “Which thirty-three?” Now Liu's ability truly appeared. From the Upper City to the Lower, he named every one of the thirty-three smaller firms whose main business was exchanging silver and copper cash. He gave the names without a pause and missed none. Even Hu felt his own memory inferior.

By now Hu had all but decided to employ him, though he would not yet say so. “Is your family in Hangzhou?” “They're all in Yuyao.” “Why don't you bring them here?” “I can't afford it yet.” “I take it you're married?” “Yes. I have two children.” “Who else is in your household?” “Both my parents are alive, and I have a younger brother at an elementary school.” “Then, including yourself, there are seven mouths to feed. That's quite a burden.” “Yes. That's why I don't dare bring them to Hangzhou. It's easier to manage in our home district.”

“If you did move them here, what would the monthly expenses be?” Hu asked. “I don't mean a life of hardship. At least a meat dish and a vegetable dish at meals, silk as well as cotton clothes—even a wife and a concubine wouldn't be excessive.” Liu laughed. “You're joking, Mr Hu.” “Then treat it as a joke. Give me a figure.” “On that basis, even ten taels a month might not be enough.” “That isn't much.” Hu continued, “Hangzhou's eight large banks are about to become nine.” “Oh?” Liu asked attentively. “Another is opening?” “Yes, very soon.” “What's its name? Where will it be?” “The name hasn't been decided, nor the location.” “Then... what do you mean?”

Hu ignored the question. “Brother Qingsheng, if this bank asked you to be its manager, would Dayuan let you go?” “What?” Liu thought he had misheard. “Please say that again.” This time he heard clearly, but could scarcely believe it. Studying Hu's face and finding no sign of a joke, he realised that his opportunity had arrived. “Dayuan would have no reason to refuse. I've got on well with everyone there. If such an opportunity came, my colleagues would be pleased for me.” “Good. Then I invite you to manage this new bank.” “You're opening it yourself, Mr Hu?” Liu was slightly surprised. “The proprietor isn't me, though you could say that I am. In any case, I have full authority. You say your expenses would be at least ten taels a month, or a hundred and twenty a year. Here's my offer: two hundred taels a year, with a bonus at year's end. What do you think?”

What more could he ask? Yet the generosity was so great that it was difficult to believe. Reading his expression, Hu understood. He excused himself, went inside, and returned with four ingots of fifty taels each, which he set before Liu. “This is for the year from this fourth month to the third month next year. Take it in advance.” “No, no!” Deeply moved, Liu pushed the silver away almost as though quarrelling. “Mr Hu, frankly, I've never even heard of anyone treating a man like this. Money can be spent, but our hearts are what matter. Just give me your instructions. Whatever you say, I'll do.” While Liu was agitated, Hu remained calm. He spoke earnestly. “Brother Qingsheng, you must take these two hundred taels today. Money gives a man confidence. With it in your hands, your mind will be settled and your thoughts more active. Any ideas you devise will naturally be better.” “That isn't what I mean...” “No more ceremony. It's money you're properly entitled to. Why refuse it? If you won't accept, I'll find it difficult to speak freely.” “Very well. Let us leave that for now and discuss the business.”

“Exactly. When you go back today, put the affairs you've handled at Dayuan in order. Our first task is to find premises. The building must be handsome and well appointed, with convenient access, and it must be in the Upper City. Ask the property brokers to show you several places. We can buy it outright or take it in pledge. Once you've chosen, tell me.” “Yes. The second task?” “Find employees. Choose whomever you think suitable.” “And the third?” “After that, it's decorating the premises, buying furniture, and so on. You handle it all. I won't interfere.” Liu considered. “I understand. Tomorrow, please open an account with a thousand taels available and give me the seal, so I can draw funds as required.” “Quite right. Write a note to Mr Zhang at Xinhe, asking him to advance a thousand taels and open the account.” This was another test, of his writing. Liu handled it easily. Hu read the note, approved it, added his written signature mark, and sent Liu away with both the note and the two hundred taels in silver.

In that single evening, Hu had completely won Liu over. Liu normally lived alone at the bank, but with so much to plan that night, he deliberately took a quiet room at an inn. He borrowed brush and inkstone from the desk, asked for two sheets of plain writing paper, and sat beneath an oil lamp listing everything he must do. The cocks were crowing by the time he finished. He lay down in his clothes for a little while and rose at daybreak. Though he had slept very little, good fortune gave him energy. Taking his silver, he went straight back to Dayuan. His colleagues, assuming that his night away had been spent with a courtesan, teased him. Liu was firm inwardly and accommodating in manner. He only smiled and began putting his accounts in order. His abacus clicked rapidly, and by noon everything was settled. After lunch, he said he was going to collect debts and went out to attend to Hu's business. First came the premises, for which he needed a property broker. At the brokers' customary teahouse meeting place, he found an acquaintance and described the layout required. He added one condition: a small residence must be rented near the bank. He intended to bring his family to Hangzhou and live close enough to attend to the business whenever needed. After arranging when to hear the broker's reply, he turned to recruiting staff. With people coming and going, he needed somewhere to meet them, and once he left Dayuan he would need lodging too. Fortunately, he had two hundred taels. He rented a small courtyard of three rooms at an inn by the month, then went to an employment agency and selected an honest, industrious general servant, who began work at the inn that day.

By dusk, Dayuan's manager, Sun Deqing, had gone home. Liu prepared four carefully chosen gifts of fresh provisions and called on him. “Oh!” Sun was bewildered. “Gifts out of the blue? What's the occasion?” “There's something on which I must ask your help...” “I know!” Sun interrupted. “I've already spoken to the proprietor. You'll get a raise after the festival. Why spend money on presents? Qingsheng, money isn't easily earned. These must have cost at least four taels—two months of your wages. Why do it?” He had completely misunderstood. Yet his kindness made Liu's news harder to deliver. Smiling, Liu said, “It seems I owe both you and the proprietor an apology.” “What?” Sun was alarmed. “What trouble have you caused? Taken on a bad debt?” “No.” Liu placed the account book he had brought before him. “Everything is settled. There isn't a single uncollectable account. Mr Sun, I'm leaving.”

“Going where?” “You'll be pleased for me when I tell you. A friend is opening a bank and wants me as manager.” “Congratulations!” Then Sun looked doubtful. “But tell me: what sort of friend? Why was there no hint of this beforehand?” “I only came upon this exceptional opportunity yesterday. You must know the man: Hu Xueyan.” “The Hu Xueyan formerly at Xinhe? He's your new employer?” Those words showed that Sun had accepted his departure. Greatly relieved, Liu smiled. “I suppose so.” “That's not right. An employer is an employer. What do you mean, ‘suppose’? I've met Hu too. Every movement of his eyebrows means another scheme. I think...” At last Sun said frankly, “He's not entirely dependable.”

“He is dependable. And if he really isn't, I'll come back. You're like an elder to me, Mr Sun. You wouldn't laugh at me.” These words pleased Sun, who nodded. “Water flows downwards, but a man seeks to rise. Going straight into a manager's position does Dayuan credit too. I only hope it doesn't become a laughing matter. If he proves unreliable, be very careful. Leave promptly and come back to us.” There had been fraudulent banks before: empty establishments that took deposits and then collapsed. That was the danger behind Sun's warning. If the proprietor fled, the manager would face legal proceedings. Nothing of the kind could happen here, Liu felt, but the warning was well meant. He had intended to suggest that the new bank establish an affiliation with Dayuan. Now there was no point in offering that overture. He answered, “I shall certainly heed your advice,” and took his leave.

From Sun's house he went to Hu's and briefly reported the day's activities. Hearing that he had rented a courtyard at an inn, Hu knew that he could act freely and decisively. He had previously feared that Liu might be too constrained to develop his abilities fully. That last doubt now disappeared. “Excellent. Go ahead. Decide anything within your authority without asking me.” “There is one thing you must decide yourself,” Liu said. “Have you settled on the firm's name? Once you have, we need someone to write it so the signboard can be made.” “Yes, that is important. But I too must consult someone wiser. I'll tell you tomorrow.”
